sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample is restricted to adults aged 25 and above (to focus on those who have completed formal schooling and to satisfy synthetic-cohort validity). The study excludes respondents born in another country (to avoid skills not influenced by the country’s educational system) and, where appropriate, drops observations on aboriginals due to distinct schooling/skills. For the synthetic-cohort analysis, the authors align age groups across IALS, ALL, and PIAAC using continuous age (in years) to select age bands that represent the same birth cohorts across survey years. They also focus on native-born, non-aboriginal populations and use re-scaled literacy outcomes to ensure comparability across IALS/ALL and the combined prose+document literacy measure in PIAAC.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper studies how adult literacy skills vary with age and how much of the cross-sectional age gradient is explained by birth-cohort differences. It combines three large-scale adult literacy assessments: IALS (1990s), ALL (2000s), and PIAAC (2011–2012), focusing on literacy as measured comparably across surveys (with IALS/ALL prose and document literacy re-scaled to match the PIAAC literacy metric). The cross-sectional analysis uses PIAAC data to estimate associations between literacy (modeled as the log of the literacy score) and age, schooling, gender, and parental background; the synthetic-cohort analysis pools IALS, ALL, and PIAAC to construct representative samples of the same birth cohorts observed at different ages across survey years. The study restricts samples to adults aged 25+ and uses provided sample weights to produce representative estimates for native-born non-aboriginal adults. The key benchmark is the direction and magnitude of age-related decline after controlling for cohort effects, and the extent to which successive cohorts show higher or lower literacy at entry into adulthood.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is not an ML predictive modeling paper: the provided text describes regression-based analyses (e.g., OLS specifications with age, schooling, and parental background, plus cohort dummies) and synthetic-cohort comparisons rather than training/evaluating machine learning algorithms. Consequently, fields related to ML techniques and predictive performance metrics are not applicable, and main_findings are intentionally left empty per the extraction rules for non-ML OECD/technical reports. The paper is still empirical and policy-relevant, but its methodological core is econometric decomposition of age vs. cohort effects rather than ML-based prediction.
